description_en: A preserved manuscript details the construction of this magnificent five-tiered temple, suggesting it was completed in approximately six months.The Ṅātāpola Mandira, recognized as Nepal's tallest temple, stands in Bhaktapur's Taumaḍhī square. Its five tiers rise from a five-tiered platform, creating a grand structure renowned not only for its height but also for its harmonious proportions and exceptional craftsmanship. While Ṅātāpola, the Newar term to mean “five tiers,” can refer to other five-tiered temples in Patan and Kirtipur, the term primarily evokes this specific temple among Nepalese, as awareness of the others in the Kathmandu valley is limited.Despite housing a statue of Siddhilakṣmī, the temple is named for its architectural style, not the goddess. The temple's steps are steep, and each level of the platform features protective stone figures. The lowest level displays two powerful male figures wielding maces and shields. Similar statues were installed by Mahanta Lokanātha Girī at the Dattātraya Temple in 1876 CE (VS 1933). Inscriptions (BKT0280_I_002_20210722_01/BKT0280_I_002_20210722_02) identify these wrestlers as Jayamala and Patā (Pratāpa), though they are commonly known as Kvatuvāḥ. Above them, in ascending order, are pairs of elephants, lions, griffons (śārdūla), and a lioness (Siṃhinī) and tigress (Vyāghrinī). The sanctum contains an almost two-meter-tall statue of Siddhilakṣmī on a stone pedestal, flanked by Mahākāla (right) and Masāna Bhairava (left). Siddhilakṣmī, who stands upon Vetāla and Bhairava, is depicted with nine faces and eighteen arms (Gutschow 2011, p. 484), although D. Śamśera (VS 2036, pp. 121-130) and P. Locana (VS 2080, p. 241) record sixteen arms. Lampstands (tvāḥdevā) stand beside Siddhilakṣmī, and a large bell, offered seventeen days after the temple's completion, hangs nearby. A drain, running north from the sanctum to the first platform level, carries away liquids offered to the goddess (Gutschow 2011, p. 484).King Bhūpatindra Malla enshrined Siddhilakṣmī in the temple as his tutelary deity. Consequently, local access has been restricted since its consecration. Only Taleju priests and members of the Karmācārya and Jośī clans are permitted entry.Toraṇas, featuring Mahiṣāsuramardinī centrally, adorn the temple doorways. The first floor's small, blind windows display statues of theaṣṭadikpālas, guardians of the eight directions. The five-tiered roof is tiled and supported by intricately carved struts depicting tantric deities. To further support the roof's weight, two additional, decoratively carved struts flank each original strut. These supplementary struts are absent from Oldfield's 1850s painting of the temple (seephoto), suggesting their later addition. D. Śamśera (VS 2036, pp. 121-130) provides a tantric interpretation of the deities depicted on the struts. A golden finial crowns the temple's summit. Its height makes at least the upper tier visible from anywhere around Bhaktapur. Small,śikhara-style Gaṇeśa shrines occupy each corner of the temple platform. D. Śamśera (VS 2036, pp. 121-130) refers to these as Diggaṇeśa. However, Gutschow (2011, p. 485) suggests that only one is Gaṇeśa, with the others representing Śiva, Nārāyaṇa, and Sūrya. As of January 2025, all four corner shrines house Gaṇeśa statues.While tradition ascribes this temple's construction to Bhūpatindra Malla, the 19th-centuryDevamālā Vaṃśāvalīembellishes the narrative, claiming that the king built the Bhavānī temple after a dream in which Bhairava of Taumaḍhī instructed him to do so. The chronicle also incorrectly dates the construction to 1756 CE (NS 876) (Yogi Naraharinatha VS 2013, p. 72). Strangely, despite the temple's grandeur, no contemporary inscription documenting its construction was discovered for some time. However, an inscription found in Tuṃthi Cuka, Bhaktapur, has since clarified the matter. This inscription, now housed in the Bhaktapur Museum, was previously used as part of the steps leading to a military office. It establishes the Ṅātāpola temple's construction date as the first day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, 1702 CE (NS 822) (P. Shrestha VS 2058, pp. 183-187). Further supporting this date, a local hymn celebrating the temple's construction includes the phrase “Nase cyāyā dathusa nase taṅāva,” which translates to “adding two in between two [and] eight” (T. Manandhara NS 1111, pp. 19-20). This phrase appears to be a coded reference to NS 822 (J. Vaidya VS 2061, p. 62).A manuscript, "Siddhāgni Koṭyāhuti Devala Pratiṣṭhā," chronicles the step-by-step construction of this temple. This document is preserved in the National Archives (NGMPP no. A 249/5, 264 folios, 17.2 x 46.5 cm). It records that construction commenced with a land purification ceremony on the 13th of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, NS 822. The temple's construction concluded later that year (1702 CE) with the finial's installation on the 1st of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha. From the land purification to the finial's placement, the construction spanned approximately six months. The continuing annual rituals performed on the day the finial was installed further corroborate the completion date.The aforementioned manuscript details the materials used in the temple's construction: 1,135,350 bricks, 102,035 floor tiles, and 27,084upā(possibly a specialized type of brick). Eight brick kilns were established outside Bhaktapur to support this project. The temple's finial, weighing 40dhārnīs, was gilded with 37tolāsof gold. Five hundred and twenty-nine hanging bells (phaygaṃ) adorned the underside of the roof. The Ṅātāpola's construction became a source of immense pride and prestige for the kingdom of Bhaktapur. King invited rulers from neighboring kingdoms, including Gorkha, Makawanpur, and Palpa, to witness the temple's progress (P. Shrestha VS 2080, p. 245). Its completion was celebrated with an unprecedented festival, featuring a grand feast for 20,000 people. These details have led scholars such as Shukrasagar, Janaklal, Niels Gutschow, and Purushottam Lochan to conclude that the temple was constructed in approximately six months. The manuscript further suggests that the Ṅātāpola was not a new construction, but rather a reconstruction. The site was previously occupied by a five-tiered structure of unknown design called “Ṅātāpula,” which was dismantled to make way for the larger temple (J. Vaidya VS 2061, p. 8). This reconstruction may have been necessitated by damage sustained by the earlier temple in the 1681 earthquake (NS 801) (P. Shrestha VS 2080, p. 241).Numerous earthquakes have shaken the Kathmandu valley since this magnificent multi-roofed temple was erected in 1702 CE (NS 822). Unfortunately, no written records document the temple's condition during tremors prior to 1934 CE (VS 1990). In both the 1934 and 2015 earthquakes, only the uppermost roof sustained damage. Subsequent renovations followed the earthquakes of 1962 CE (VS 2019), 1999 CE (VS 2056), and the most recent tremor.Because the temple's principal deity was the royal family's tutelary deity, public access is restricted. Consequently, the temple's inner sanctum remains closed, and daily religious observances are not conducted. The temple's anniversary is celebrated on the 1st of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, marking its completion. On this occasion, Brahmins, Karmācāryas, and Jośīs conduct special rituals within the temple. Following these rites, a white flag bearing a crescent moon is raised atop the finial. The next day, a group of Brahmins, Karmācāryas, and Jośīs continue the tradition of performingthāpūjā, a special worship ceremony, commemorating the establishment of Ṅātāpola at the Taleju temple.The Ṅātāpola temple's influence extends beyond Bhaktapur's architecture, permeating local folklore and cultural values. Proverbs, folk songs, and beliefs associated with the temple have become ingrained in Bhaktapur's traditions. A single hanging bell remains beneath the temple's eaves, and locals believe that its ringing, stirred by the wind, foretells heavy rainfall (P. Shrestha VS 2080, p. 247). The 1934 earthquake, which damaged the upper roof, inspired a still-popular rhyming proverb: "Ṅātāpola chatā madu, Bhailaḥdyaḥ patā madu." This translates to "One roof of Ṅātāpola [was lost], and the Bhairava temple was completely gone," vividly illustrating the earthquake's impact.The Ṅātāpola also features in a hymn attributed to King Raṇajita Malla, composed after the loss of his kingdom. The hymn expresses a poignant longing, lamenting, "I was born a dove, yearning to see Ṅātāpola, but the Khasa sons shot me down" (P. Shrestha VS 2080, pp. 151-152). This hymn is traditionally sung throughout Bhaktapur during theBiskāḥ Jātrāfestival (local resident, Basukala, male, age 53).
description_ne: पाँच तलाको यस भव्य मन्दिर बन्दै गर्दा चरणवद्ध घटनाको टिपोट गरिएको एक ग्रन्थ सुरक्षित छ जसबाट यो करिब छ महिनामै बनेको देखिन्छ ।नेपालकै सर्वोच्च उचाई भएको ङातापोल मन्दिर भक्तपुरको तौमढी टोलमा अवस्थित छ । खुला परिसरमाझ पाँचतहको पेटीमाथि पाँचै तलामा उभिएको मन्दिर उचाईका दृष्टिले मात्र नभई मिल्दो वास्तु अनुपात र उत्कृष्ट शिल्पीका कारण पनि निकै भव्य देखापर्छ । यो भक्तपुरको मात्र नभई देशकै सबैभन्दा अग्लो मन्दिर हो । पाटन र कान्तिपुरमा पनि पाँचतले मन्दिर भए तापनि ती कतिपय सर्वसाधारणलाई थाहापत्तै छैन ।  नेपाली जनमानसमा ‘पाँचतले मन्दिर’ शब्दले भक्तपुरकै मन्दिरको झल्को दिने गर्दछ । ‘पाँच तहको छाना” समास भई नेपालभाषामा ‘ङातापोल’ शब्द बनेको हो । यसको अनुवादित रूप ‘पाँचतले’ पनि त्यतिकै प्रचलनमा आएको छ । सिद्धिलक्ष्मीको मूर्ति स्थापित मन्दिर भए तापनि यसको नाम देवीको नामबाट नभई वास्तुगत विशेषताकै आधारमा रहन गएको छ । मन्दिरको सिँढी निकै ठाडो छ र त्यहाँ पेटीको तह अनुसार रक्षार्थ राखिएका शिलाका प्रतिमा छन् । सबैभन्दा तल्लो तहमा गदा र ढाल लिएका बलिष्ठ दुई पुरुषपात्र बसेका छन् । दत्तात्रय मन्दिरमा यसै समान दुई पात्रका प्रतिमा महन्त लोकनाथ गिरीले विसं १९३३ (सन् १८७६) मा स्थापना गरेका थिए ।  ती पहलमानहरूलाई अभिलेखमा जयमल र पता (प्रताप) नाम दिइएको छ (BKT0280_I_002_20210722_01/BKT0280_I_002_20210722_02) । बोलीचालीमा भने यिनलाई क्वतुवाः भन्ने चलन छ । यी भन्दा माथिल्लो तहमा क्रमश हात्ती, सिंह, शार्दूल र सिंहिनी-व्याघ्रिनीका मूर्ति छन् । गर्भगृहमा शिलाको वेदिकामाथि शिलाकै करिब २ मीटर अग्लो सिद्धिलक्ष्मीको प्रतिमा छ । उनको दायाँ महाकाल र बायाँ मसान भैरव रहेका छन् । बेताल र भैरवमाथि उभिएकी सिद्धिलक्ष्मीको ९ वटा मुखाकृति र १८ हात छन् (Gutschow 2011, p. 484) । D. Śamśera (VS 2036, pp. 121-130) र P. Locana (VS 2080, p. 241) ले भने मूर्तिमा १६ हात मात्र भएको बताएका छन् । सिद्धिलक्ष्मीको दायाँ-बायाँ त्वाःदेवा पनि खडा छन् भने मन्दिर निर्माणको १७ दिनपश्चात् चढाइएको एक ठुलो घण्ट झुण्ड्याइएको छ । देवीलाई अर्पित तरल पदार्थको निकासका लागि पहिलो तहको पेटीसम्म (उत्तरतिर) डुँड (drainage) बनाइएको छ (Gutschow 2011, p. 484) ।भूपतिन्द्र मल्लले स्वइष्टदेवीका रूपमा यहाँ सिद्धिलक्ष्मी देवी स्थापना गरेका हुन् । यसर्थ यहाँ सुरुदेखि स्थानीयलाई प्रवेश निषेध छ । मन्दिरभित्र तलेजुका पुजारी, कर्माचार्य र जोशी खलकले मात्र प्रवेश पाउँछ । मन्दिरका ढोकामाथि तोरण चढाइएका छन् जसको केन्द्रमा महिषासुरमर्दिनी छन् । पहिलो तलामा भएका स-साना झ्यालमा (blind windows) अष्टदिक्पालका मूर्ति छन् । मन्दिरका पाँचै तहका छाना झिंगटीले छाइएको छ जसलाई थाम्न विविध तान्त्रिक देवदेवीका मूर्ति अङ्कित टुँडाल प्रयोगमा छन् । छानाको भारी वजन थाम्न प्रत्येक टुँडालका दायाँ-बायाँ अतिरिक्त दुई टुँडाल थपिएका छन् जसको सतहमा फुलबुट्टा कुँदिएको छ । Oldfield ले सन् १८५० को दशकमा यस मन्दिरको चित्र कोर्दा यहाँ यी अतिरिक्त टुँडाल देखा पर्दैनन् (चित्र हेर्नुहोस्) । यसर्थ यी पछिमात्र थपिएको बुझिन्छ । यस मन्दिरको टुँडालका देव-देवीको तान्त्रिक व्याख्या D. Śamśera (VS 2036, pp. 121-130) ले गरेका छन् । मन्दिरको उचो तलामा सुवर्ण गजुर चढाइएको छ । मन्दिरको उचाईका कारण भक्तपुर नगर बाहिर चौरैतिरबाट मन्दिरको कम्तिमा माथिल्लो तह देख्न सकिन्छ । मन्दिरको पेटीको चारैतिरको कोणमा साना शिखराकार गणेश देवल बनाइएका छन् । यी गणेशलाई D. Śamśera (VS 2036, pp. 121-130)  ले दिग्गणेश भनेका छन् । Gutschow (2011, p. 485) ले भने यी चारै गणेश नभई बाँकी तीन शिव, नारायण र सूर्य मानेका छन् । हाल (जनवरी २०२५) यी सबै देवलमा गणेश मूर्ति हालिएका छन् ।यस मन्दिरको निर्माण भक्तपुरका प्रसिद्ध राजा भूपतिन्द्र मल्लले गराएका थिए । देवमाला वंशावलीमा भने निर्माणकार्यलाई दैवीकरण गर्दै तौमढीका भैरवले सपनामा राजालाई आज्ञा भए बमोजिम भवानीको मन्दिर थपेको भनिएको छ । निर्माण मिति पनि नेसं ८७६ (सन् १७५६) भनी गलत जानकारी दिइएको छ (Yogī Naraharinātha VS 2013, p. 72) । भव्य मन्दिर भए तापनि यसको निर्माणसंग सम्बन्धित अभिलेख नपाइनु अनौठो छ । तर भक्तपुरकै तुंथि चुकमा फेला परेको एक अभिलेखमा यसको निर्माणमिति किटान गरिएको छ । सैन्य कार्यालय छिर्न बनाइएको सिँढीमा प्रयोग भएको ढुङ्गामा उक्त अभिलेख देखिएको थियो । हाल यस अभिलेखलाई भक्तपुर संग्राहलयमा सुरक्षित राखिएको छ । सो अभिलेखबाट नेसं ८२२ (सन् १७०२) आषाढ शुक्ल प्रतिपदाको दिन ङातापोल मन्दिर बनेको तथ्य खुल्दछ (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2058, pp. 183-87) । भक्तपुरमा गाइने एक भजनमा पनि ङातापोल मन्दिर निर्माणको महिमा पोखिएको छ । उक्त गीतमा मन्दिरको निर्माण मितिलाई संकेत गर्दै ‘नसे च्याया दथुस नसे तङाव’ भनिएको छ (T. Mānandhara NS 1111, pp. 19-20) । उक्त अभिव्यक्तिले पनि नेसं ८२२ लाई नै जनाएको देखिन्छ (J. Vaidya VS 2061, p. 62) ।यस मन्दिरको निर्माणमा भएका चरणवद्ध घटनालाई समेटी ‘सिद्धाग्नि कोट्याहुति देवल प्रतिष्ठा’ नामक ग्रन्थ लेखिएको थियो । उक्त ग्रन्थ राष्ट्रिय अभिलेखालयमा सुरक्षित छ (NGMPP no. A 249/5, 264 folios, 17.2 x 46.5 cm) । ग्रन्थमा नेसं ८२२ (सन् १७०१) पौष कृष्ण त्रयोदशीका दिनमा भूमिशोधन गरी निर्माणारम्भ गरिएको कुरा उल्लेख छ । यसै सालको (सन् १७०२) आषाढ शुदि प्रतिपदामा गजुर स्थापना गरी समापन गरिएको थियो । भूमिशोधनदेखि गजुर चढाइएको अवधिलाई हिसाब गर्दा करिब छ महिनामा मन्दिर बनेको देखिन्छ । आषाढ शुदि १ मै मन्दिर सम्पन्न भएको हो भन्ने कुराको पुष्टि हालसम्म यसै दिन पारी गर्दै आएको वर्षवर्द्धन पूजाले पनि पुष्टि गर्छ । माथि उल्लेखित ग्रन्थको उल्लेखन अनुसार मन्दिरका खातिर ११३५३५० इँटा, १०२०३५ चिकंअप्पा, २७०८४ उपा ? खरिद भएको थियो । भक्तपुर नगर बाहिर आठ स्थानमा अगःचा (इँटाभत्ता) बनेका थिए । मन्दिरमा ४० धार्नीको गजुर प्रयोग भएको र सोमाथि ३७ तोला सुन खर्चेर जलप लगाइएको थियो । मन्दिरका छानामुनि कुल ५२९ फय्‌गं झुण्ड्याइएका थिए । ङातापोल निर्माण परियोजना भक्तपुर राज्यकै गौरव र इज्जतको विषय बन्न पुगेको थियो । तत्कालीन राजनैतिक वृत्तमा भक्तपुरनिकट गोरखा, मकवानपुर, पाल्पा आदि राज्यका राजाहरू निम्त्याई निर्माणाधीन मन्दिर देखाइएको थियो (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 245) । मन्दिरको निर्माणकार्य समापन भक्तपुरको लागि अभूतपूर्व महोत्सव बनेको थियो । यस अवसरमा तःभ्वय् (देय्‌भ्वय्) आयोजन गरी २० हजार जनालाई भोज खुवाइएको थियो । यी उल्लेखित तथ्यका आधारमा  शुक्रसागर, जनकलाल, Niels Gutschow, पुरुषोत्तमलोचन आदि विद्वानले यो मन्दिर करिब ६ महिनाको छोटो अवधिमै बनेको कुरा स्वीकारेका छन् । यो मन्दिर नवनिर्माण नभई पुनर्निर्माण भएको संकेत पनि उक्त ग्रन्थबाट मिल्छ । हाल मन्दिर उभिएको स्थानमा पहिले नै ‘ङातापुल’ भनिने कुनै आकारको पाँचतले मन्दिर थियो । उक्त मन्दिरलाई विस्थापन गरी अर्को विशाल मन्दिर उठाइएको हो (J. Vaidya VS 2061, p. 8) । नेसं ८०१ (सन् १६८१) को भूकम्पमा क्षति भएको पहिलेको मन्दिरलाई भत्काई नयाँ बनाइएको पनि हुन सक्दछ (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 241) ।नेसं ८२२ (सन् १७०२) मा सर्वोच्च बहुछाने मन्दिर बनेपश्चात् उपत्यकामा विविध भूकम्पहरू गएका छन् । ती भूकम्पमध्ये विसं १९९० (सन् १९३४) पूर्वका भूकम्पमा मन्दिरको स्थिति के-कस्तो रह्यो भनी जान्न सकिने कुनै लिखित प्रमाण छैन । विसं १९९० (सन् १९३४) र विसं २०७२ (सन् २०१५) का दुबै महाभूकम्पमा माथिल्लो छानोमा मात्र क्षति पुगेको थियो । विसं २०१९, विसं २०५६ र पछिल्लो भूकम्पपश्चात् मन्दिरको जीर्णोद्धार भएको छ ।राजाका स्वइष्टदेवी भएबाट यस मन्दिरमा सर्वसाधारणलाई प्रवेश निषेध छ । यसर्थ मन्दिरको गर्भगृह बन्द रहन्छ र यहाँ सामान्य दिनहरूमा धार्मिक गतिविधि देखा पर्दैन । मन्दिरमा यसको निर्माण सम्पन्न तिथि अर्थात् आषाढ शुक्ल प्रतिपदाका दिन वर्षवर्द्धन हुने गर्दछ । उक्त वर्षवर्द्धनका दौरान ब्राह्मण, कर्माचार्य र जोशीले मन्दिरमा पूजापाठ गर्दछन् । यसपश्चात् मन्दिरको गजुरमा सेतो सतहमा चन्द्र अङ्कित झण्डा चढाउने गरिन्छ । यसको भोलिपल्ट ब्राह्मण, कर्माचार्य र जोशीको समूहले तलेजुमा ङातापोल स्थापनाको थापुजा गर्ने चलन यद्यपि कायम छ । भक्तपुरको स्थापत्य क्षेत्रमा मात्र नभई लोकमानस र यहाँको मूल्य मान्यतामा पनि ङातापोलको प्रभाव देख्न सकिन्छ । भक्तपुरमा यस मन्दिरसँग जोडिएर लोकोक्ति, लोकगीत एवं विश्वासहरू विकास भएका छन् । मन्दिरको छानामुनि एक फय्‌गं बचेको स्थिति छ । भक्तपुरवासीमा यस फय्‌गं हावाको प्रवाहले बज्न थालेमा ठुलो वर्षा हुने लोकविश्वास छ (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, p. 247) । विसं १९९० (सन् १९३४) मा माथिल्लो छानो भत्किएको प्रसंग कैद गरी एक लोकोक्ति बनेको थियो जुन हालसम्म पनि प्रचलित छ । अन्त्यानुप्रास मिलाइएको उक्त लोकोक्तिमा “ङातापोल छता मदु, भैलःद्यः पता मदु” भनिएको छ । यसको अर्थ भूकम्पका दौरान “ङातापोलको एक तला र सँगैको भैरव मन्दिर पूर्णतः गायब भयो” भन्ने हुन्छ । भक्तपुर राज्य गुमाएपश्चात् रणजित मल्लले लेखेको विश्वास गरिने एक भजनमा पनि ङातापोलको प्रसंग परेको छ । जसमा “ङातापोल हेर्ने इच्छाले परेवाको जन्म लिएको तर चण्डाल प्रवृत्तिका खसका सन्तानले बन्दुक पड्काइ मारे” भनी मर्मस्पर्शी भाव पोखिएको छ (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2080, pp. 151-152) । यो भजन बिस्काः जात्राका दौरान भक्तपुरभर गाउने चलन छ (local resident, Bāsukalā, male, age 53) ।
monument_assessment: Good (very few light surface damages, renovated or repaired)

historical_events.event_name: Dispatching of woodcutters to cut down tree
historical_events.event_description: The woodcutters were dispatched to cut down the trees in the jungle for timbers to build the temple.
Timbers of thesāla(shorea robusta) variety were obtained from various places like Nālā, Panautī, Caukoṭa, Vābhudvã, and Yãlādvã for building the temple.

historical_events.event_name: Beginning of making of temple bells
historical_events.event_description: The crafting of the temple bells (phaygaṃ) to be hung below the eaves of the temple roof started from this day onward.

historical_events.event_name: Beginning of works related to timbers and foundation
historical_events.event_description: Carpenters began their woodworks. Digging the pits for the foundation also began from this day onward.
The temple named “Ṅātāpula” was demolished to build a new “Ṅātāpola” temple.
From this day onward, the brick-firing process began in various locations throughout Bhaktapur. Brick firing continued uninterrupted until the 11th of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.
The digging for the temple’s foundation commenced from this day onward.
The foundation stone was laid, marking the beginning of the temple’s construction. The foundation stones were consecrated, and multiple levels of plinths were built.
The crafting of the temple’s finial commenced.

historical_events.event_name: Obtainment of woods form various places
historical_events.event_description: Timbers of thethāsĩandmūsĩvariety were obtained from Vābhu and Nhaygāṃ (lit. seven villages, which are Banepā, Nālā, Sāṃgā, Dhulikhela, Panautī, Caukoṭa, and Khaḍpu) for the construction of the temple.
To build the temple, groups led by soldiers, including Rājaphauḍa, Dhana Khārisā, Śaṃkarasiṃ, and Bhāyadeva, brought in the finest quality stones from Kotkhālvahaṃ (Hāttīvana).
The topmost roof of the temple was installed.

historical_events.event_name: Completion of roofing on topmost tier and performance of propitiatory rituals
historical_events.event_description: The topmost roof tier was completely tiled with traditional materials. Supplies for raising the ceremonial banner (betālipatāḥ) atop the finial were sent from the Nhaygāṃ (literally, "seven villages") cluster east of Bhaktapur. Following the completion of the top tier's roofing, special propitiatory rituals (śānti-svasti) were performed, and the necessary ritual paintings were commissioned.

During the construction of the temple, King Bhūpatindra Malla performed akoṭyāhutiyajña, a fire oblation of 10 million oblations. He gifted a golden crown to the priest who performed the rituals. This crown is still safely kept by the Karmācārya priests of the Tripura Vidyāpīṭha Āgama.

The statue of Siddhilakṣmī, the main deity, was established inside the sanctum on this day. The finial was also installed on top of the uppermost tier on the occasion, marking the completion of the construction. The three miniature temples were also built around the temple.
On this day, a bell was offered to the temple. The fact that there was a large bell inside the temple is known from a survey conducted by Surendra Jośī in 1977 CE.

historical_events.event_name: Collapse of upper tier in 1934 earthquakes
historical_events.event_description: The uppermost tier of the temple collapsed in the 1934 earthquakes. The damage inspired a still-popular rhyming proverb: "Ṅātāpola chatā madu, Bhailaḥdyaḥ patā madu." This translates to "One roof of Ṅātāpola [was lost], and the Bhairava temple was completely gone," vividly illustrating the earthquake's impact.

A significant renovation was carried out in 1963 CE. During this renovation, the brick face of the stepped plinth was replaced with red-colored cement mortar, and the face of the sanctum was also renewed.

The Bhaktapur Municipality renovated the temple, aiming at reducing the roof load. The thickness of the mud layer was decreased, the spacing of the rafters was doubled, and the cross-section of the rafters was reduced. Additionally, the two central struts on the lowest level facing south, thetoraṇafacing north and west, the northern bracket of the western door, and the 36 plaques on the capitals and lintels were all renewed.
The uppermost roof sustained damage in the 2015 earthquakes.

Following earthquake damage, the Bhaktapur Municipality undertook a comprehensive renovation of the temple. The public participated extensively in volunteer efforts, and significant financial and material contributions were received, enabling the project's completion by the end of 2020 CE.
